# Career Arc — Age at Release as a Dimension

> The first build from **What the Graph Could Answer** (Spike, Approved), whose recommended first step was: *"Make **`AgeAtRelease`** a first-class dimension — filter, sort, group. Everything needed exists, it is display-only today."*
> 
> Operator's framing: *"Information about actors as they age is potentially an interesting data point and may be an interesting way to view videos on an actor's profile page."*
## The mechanism, restated
⭐ **Every edge that touches a video inherits that video's release date for free.** That is the whole feature: `video_performer` + `Asset.releaseDate` + `EntityProfile.birthDate` is a career arc, with **no new schema, no new edge, and no new data**. The pieces existed and were not connected.
## What was built
### 1. Release Date as a sort
`AssetSort.Option.releaseDate`. The library's own chronology rather than the operator's — `Date Added` says only what order a collection was assembled in, which is a fact about the collector.
⚠️ **Undated videos sort LAST in ascending order.** They are not "very old", they are unknown, and leading a career view with them opens it on the records that say nothing about it. Ties fall back to series order so an episode sequence released on one day still reads in order. An empty-string date counts as unknown — treating it as a date would sort those records to the front of every chronological view.
### 2. `CareerArc` — the grouping
Pure, in `LibraryCore`, because the honesty rules are decisions rather than layout.
| Rule | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Sections ascend by age | A career is read forwards |
| Unknown ages sort **last** | They say nothing about the arc; opening on them buries the part that does |
| A section is **approximate** if ANY member is | A section header is a claim, and it cannot claim more precision than its least precise entry |
| Approximate reads **"Around 25"**, exact reads **"Age 25"** | An age from a birth YEAR is right to within a year and no better — whether the birthday had happened yet is unknown |
| A release before the birth is **unknown**, not negative | `AgeAtReleaseCalculator` already refuses to say something wrong; this preserves that |
| Needs **more than one KNOWN** age to show | One age is a single section with a number on it, which is not an arc; all-unknown is a header over the whole page saying nothing |
Also `evidencedAgeRange` — the span the library actually proves, which is the input to a self-audit check the spike called for: where it disagrees with the recorded `careerStartYear`, either the record or a match is wrong. Nothing consumes it yet.
### 3. The actor profile page
Collapsible per-age sections, the same pattern now shared by the season-grouped series grid and the studio family view — three groupings, one control.
Shown when: a single performer is selected, the sort is **Release Date**, and there is more than one known age. Same shape as `showSeasonSections` — one entity, the matching sort, more than one group.
⚠️ **A performer's page now defaults to Release Date sort**, exactly as a series page defaults to episode order and for the same reason: it is the ordering that makes the page mean something, and it puts the arc in front of the operator rather than behind a sort menu they would have to know to open. Reversible from the sort menu.
Sections are computed from the **displayed** assets, so they re-split as filters narrow rather than describing a career the page is not showing.
### 4. Age at release as a filter
`AssetFilterCriteria.minAgeAtRelease` / `maxAgeAtRelease`, with a section in the filter builder. **The library's first filter on a fact no single record holds** — it needs the video's release date and the performer's birth date together, which is precisely the join the graph exists to make cheap.
🚨 **Every possible age must satisfy the bounds, not just the headline number.** An age derived from a birth YEAR is either that number or one less, because whether the birthday had come round is unknown. Filtering on `years` would report an approximate 18 as certainly 18 and include a record that might not qualify — the failure the spike named exactly.
⚠️ **This is the conservative reading and it excludes some records that do qualify.** The asymmetry is intended: a filter that wrongly includes states something the data does not support, while one that wrongly excludes merely shows less. `AgeAtRelease.displayText` already renders an approximate age as a range for the same reason.
Consequence worth knowing: a performer with a full birth date matches where one with only a birth year does not, at the same headline age. That is the data being honest about itself, not an inconsistency.
A video whose ages cannot be established does **not** match. The filter asks a question about age; a record that cannot answer it has not answered yes.
One qualifying performer is enough, matching how every other actor-metadata filter here behaves. Zero means "unset" and reads **Any**, since an age bound of zero would exclude nothing while looking like a real setting. Filters saved before these fields existed still decode — pinned by a test against a stored payload.
## Not built yet
- The self-audit checks (section E of the spike), which `evidencedAgeRange` now makes cheap.
- Studio-side career-stage analysis (section B), which needs the same join from the other end.
- Tag trajectory over time (section C).
## Verification
LibraryCore 1,072 tests, 0 failures — 31 new across `CareerArc`, the release-date sort and the age filter. macOS and iOS build. D9 clean.
⚠️ Not verified against a populated library: the drive was not attached, so the arc has never been rendered against a real filmography. Worth checking that the section count is useful rather than overwhelming — a performer with a fifteen-year career produces fifteen sections, and if that reads badly the natural fallback is grouping by a band of years rather than by single years.
